transforms.name: grayscale
transforms.how: Input is a 224x224 uint8 RGB PIL image. Compute img.convert('L').convert('RGB'). This uses ITU-R BT.601 luma, L = (299*R + 587*G + 114*B)/1000, and copies L into all three channels.
transforms.removes: All chromatic information: hue, saturation and colour contrast between regions of equal luminance.
transforms.keeps: Luminance at every pixel, so edges, contours, shading, texture, spatial frequency content and layout are unchanged.
transforms.source: Geirhos et al. 2018, 'Generalisation in humans and deep neural networks', NeurIPS (greyscale condition). Luma weights from ITU-R BT.601.

transforms.name: low_pass
transforms.how: Convert the image to x = float64 array of shape (224,224,3) in [0,255]. Compute y = scipy.ndimage.gaussian_filter(x, sigma=(4,4,0), mode='reflect'), which blurs each channel with a Gaussian of 4 px standard deviation. The amplitude falls to half at about 0.047 cycles/px, roughly 10.5 cycles per image. Output np.clip(np.round(y),0,255).astype(np.uint8).
transforms.removes: High spatial frequencies: fine edges, thin lines, fine texture, small details and sharp boundaries.
transforms.keeps: Coarse structure: large blobs, mean colour and local colour, overall layout and low-frequency shading.
transforms.source: Geirhos et al. 2018, NeurIPS (low-pass condition). Spatial frequency filtering in vision science: Campbell & Robson 1968; Schyns & Oliva 1994.

transforms.name: high_pass
transforms.how: x = float64 array (224,224,3) in [0,255]. Compute y = x - scipy.ndimage.gaussian_filter(x, sigma=(4,4,0), mode='reflect') + x.mean(axis=(0,1), keepdims=True), which adds back each channel's own mean. The output is np.clip(np.round(y),0,255).astype(np.uint8). This uses the same sigma as low_pass, so the two are exact complements: low_pass + high_pass = x + mean before clipping. Do not rescale the contrast.
transforms.removes: Low spatial frequencies below about 10 cycles per image: smooth shading, gradual colour and luminance gradients, large uniform regions and coarse blob structure. As a side effect, RMS contrast is lower.
transforms.keeps: Fine edges, contours, thin lines, fine texture and each channel's mean colour.
transforms.source: Geirhos et al. 2018, NeurIPS (high-pass condition). Schyns & Oliva 1994, Psychological Science (hybrid images).

transforms.name: phase_scramble
transforms.how:
x = float64 array (224,224,3) in [0,255].
1. Draw the noise with rng = np.random.default_rng(0) and set theta = np.angle(np.fft.fft2(rng.standard_normal((224,224)))).
2. Set theta[0,0] = 0 so the mean is preserved.
3. For each channel c, compute F = np.fft.fft2(x[:,:,c]) and y[:,:,c] = np.real(np.fft.ifft2(np.abs(F) * np.exp(1j*(np.angle(F) + theta)))).
4. Output np.clip(np.round(y),0,255).astype(np.uint8).
All three channels get the same theta, so the phase differences between channels stay the same. Every image uses the same seed and the same theta.
transforms.removes: All spatial structure carried by Fourier phase: edges, contours, object shape, the positions of parts and local feature alignment.
transforms.keeps: Each channel's Fourier amplitude spectrum, meaning power at each spatial frequency and orientation. Also keeps mean colour, overall colour palette, RMS contrast (up to clipping) and correlations between channels.
transforms.source: Oppenheim & Lim 1981, 'The importance of phase in signals', Proc. IEEE. Geirhos et al. 2018, NeurIPS (phase noise condition). Widely used to make control stimuli in vision science.

transforms.name: patch_shuffle_4x4
transforms.how: Split the 224x224x3 array into a 4x4 grid of 56x56 tiles, numbered in row-major order t = 4*row + col. Build the output by placing source tile perm[p] at output position p (row-major), using the fixed permutation perm = [10,7,13,0,15,2,8,5,3,12,1,14,6,9,4,11]. No tile stays in its original place, and no two originally adjacent tiles stay adjacent in the same relative position. Pixel values are not changed.
transforms.removes: Global configuration: arrangement of parts beyond 56 px, object shape at larger scales, scene layout and long-range contours. It also adds artificial straight edges at tile seams.
transforms.keeps: All local content inside each 56x56 tile: local texture, colour, small parts, local edges and their orientation. Pixel statistics across the image are exactly preserved.
transforms.source: Grill-Spector et al. 1998, Neuron (scrambled-object controls). Zhang & Zhu 2019, 'Interpreting adversarially trained CNNs', ICLR (patch shuffling). Brendel & Bethge 2019, ICLR (BagNets, local-feature models).

transforms.name: rotate_90
transforms.how: Compute y = np.rot90(x, k=1, axes=(0,1)), a lossless 90-degree counter-clockwise rotation. The image is square, so nothing is cropped or padded.
transforms.removes: Absolute orientation: every edge, line and texture is rotated by 90 degrees, so horizontal becomes vertical. It also removes the upright, gravity-aligned layout of objects and scenes, for example sky at the top and ground at the bottom.
transforms.keeps: Every pixel value, colour, spatial frequency content, contrast, local texture apart from its orientation, and the relative arrangement of parts up to a rigid rotation.
transforms.source: Geirhos et al. 2018, NeurIPS (rotation conditions 90, 180 and 270 degrees). Engstrom et al. 2019, ICML (spatial robustness of CNNs). Orientation tuning: Hubel & Wiesel 1962.

transforms.name: edge_map
transforms.how:
1. Set g = np.asarray(img.convert('L'), dtype=float64), then g = scipy.ndimage.gaussian_filter(g, sigma=2).
2. Compute gx = scipy.ndimage.sobel(g, axis=1), gy = scipy.ndimage.sobel(g, axis=0) and mag = np.hypot(gx, gy).
3. Mark e = mag > np.percentile(mag, 90), so the strongest 10% of pixels count as edges.
4. Output black edges on a white background: out = np.where(e, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8), copied into all three channels.
transforms.removes: Colour, shading, surface reflectance, texture inside regions, edge contrast magnitude and contrast polarity. Mean luminance is replaced by a white background.
transforms.keeps: The location and orientation of the strongest luminance edges, which give the outline shape of objects and the main internal contours.
transforms.source: Geirhos et al. 2019, 'ImageNet-trained CNNs are biased towards texture', ICLR (edge stimuli). Canny 1986. Sobel gradient operator (standard practice).

transforms.name: luminance_polarity_inversion
transforms.how: x = float64 array (224,224,3) in [0,255]. Compute L = 0.299*x[:,:,0] + 0.587*x[:,:,1] + 0.114*x[:,:,2], then y = x + (255 - 2*L)[:,:,None]. Output np.clip(np.round(y),0,255).astype(np.uint8). This is exactly the same as converting to BT.601 full-range YCbCr, setting Y to 255 - Y, keeping Cb and Cr, and converting back. Highly saturated pixels can be clipped.
transforms.removes: The sign of luminance contrast: light-on-dark becomes dark-on-light. Shading direction and luminance-defined shape-from-shading cues are reversed.
transforms.keeps: The positions and orientations of luminance edges, the luminance amplitude spectrum (except the DC term), chromatic (Cb and Cr) content, geometry and layout.
transforms.source: Galper 1970, Psychonomic Science (contrast negation). Kemp et al. 1996, Perception (separating luminance negation from hue negation). Hosseini et al. 2017, 'On the limitation of CNNs in recognizing negative images', ICMLA.
